title: 1MW No. 320: Understanding The Motivation Gap
author: Greg McKeown
summary: Greg McKeown summarizes new research on why people abandon even their most important resolutions, despite overwhelmingly saying they choose goals for long-term importance rather than momentary enjoyment. The study, which tracked 2,000 Americans across a year of resolution-keeping, found that how enjoyable the pursuit felt in the moment predicted persistence better than how important the outcome was rated to be. A follow-up experiment on a health app confirmed the mechanism causally: framing a mundane task as fun rather than merely useful increased engagement by more than 25 percent within a day. McKeown's practical takeaway is that leaders and individuals should stop relying solely on long-term stakes to sustain motivation and instead deliberately import some of a goal's reward into the present moment, pairing hard work with something already enjoyable.
points: Cites a year-long study of 2,000 resolution-makers showing that how enjoyable the pursuit felt predicted persistence better than how important the goal's long-term outcome was rated.
Notes the disconnect between stated values and behavior: 90 percent of people say they choose goals for long-term importance, yet enjoyment, not importance, drove actual follow-through.
Cites an experimental health-app study where framing a task as 'fun' rather than merely 'useful' increased usage by more than 25 percent in 24 hours, establishing a causal mechanism.
Offers a reframed strategy: instead of only stating why a goal matters, deliberately pair the hard part of pursuing it with something already enjoyable to bring some reward into the present.
quotes: The experience of pursuing the goal was a better predictor of whether people kept going than the value of the outcome.
In a follow-up study, 90 percent said they would select a resolution because it was important in the long run rather than because it was enjoyable in the moment.

One group was encouraged to see it as a fun way to make surprising discoveries. Another was encouraged to focus on the useful information it provided. Over the next 24 hours, the first group used the app to scan more than 25 percent more products.
The long-term reward gives us a reason to start. Bringing some of that reward into the present gives us a reason to keep going.
Essential activities don't have to be enjoyed only in retrospect.
